The driver had no traffic or incident excuse: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band readings were band 4 (30–39 km/h) on AYE and CTE, not band 1 or 2 severe congestion, so no segment is exempt under RD-4.

The rider's chat contains no agreement to any reroute: the only rider message is an arrival note about a red jacket at the lobby, and the driver admits he rerouted on his own GPS ('it rerouted me') — the change was not agreed before leaving the optimal route.

Because no segment is exempt, the unexempt off-route kilometre (0.77 km) is refundable under RD-2's meter formula: 0.77 km × the trip's own per-km rate of $17.47 ÷ 12.4 km = $1.41/km, i.e. $1.0857, rounded to $1.09.

The remaining billed excess is not claimed: the $2.30 excess-distance charge covers the full 1.6 km gap (F1) while the unexempt segment is only 0.77 km (F3), and RD-2 limits recovery to the unexempt segment's extra_km, so only $1.09 is requested.
No waiting fee or unannounced add-on remains in dispute: waiting was charged $0.00 and the total $27.76 is base $3.90 + distance $17.47 + time $4.92 + platform $1.47 at 1.0× surge.
This is not a flag_account case for the driver: the driver's 90-day record shows route disputes upheld = 0, so the RD-6 'repeated' threshold is not met, and I do not request an account flag.

weaknesses: The gap between billed and optimal distance is 1.6 km (F1, F4) but the unexempt off-route segment adds only 0.77 km (F3), so the driver can argue the rest of the difference is normal GPS/map-matching variance and that RD-2 caps recovery at the segment sum — this is exactly why I request only $1.09.

The driver's statement (F9) says the reroute came from the navigation app showing the fastest route, and traffic bands 4 on AYE and CTE (F10, F11) show moderate congestion, which the driver will use to argue a 'reasonable cause' detour even though F12 shows no incident and band 4 is far from RD-4(b)'s band 1–2.

claims.assertion: The passenger's own chat message at 09:35 asks the driver to 'find you at the lobby' — the only rider-side routing-type instruction in the record — so any deviation was not the result of a rider-named stop or route change request under RD-3(a).

The GPS track shows exactly one off-route segment, 09:49–09:52, which added 0.77 km (2.15 km driven vs 1.38 km optimal); the remaining part of the +1.6 km trip excess (F1) is not attributable to any measured off-route segment and must not be charged to the driver.

For this RydeTAXI trip the extra billable distance is 0.77 km, which at the per-km rate of $1.41/km (F4: $2.30 for 1.6 km) equals a maximum meter overcharge of 0.77 × $1.41 ≈ $1.09, not the full $2.30 excess the rider claims.

No traffic incident was recorded anywhere near the route during the trip window (F12) and the only speed-band records are expressway bands of 30–39 km/h (F10, F11) on roads that are not tied to the replaced optimal stretch, so the reroute satisfies neither RD-4(a) nor RD-4(b) and the driver cannot claim the congestion exemption.

The driver's statement that he simply followed his GPS (F9) is unsupported by any pre-departure route agreement with the rider in the chat record, so RD-5 does not exempt the segment; the driver's exposure is therefore capped at the single measured segment rather than the whole distance gap.

There is no justification for any account-level action against the driver: the profile shows 889 trips in 90 days, rating 4.8, and zero upheld route disputes in the last 90 days (F15), so the RD-6 'repeated route deviation' precondition (≥ 1 previously upheld route dispute) is not met.

No other fare line item is contested and none is unsupported: the total of $27.76 (F6) contains only base, distance, time at 18.9 min (F2), platform fee $1.47 and $0.00 waiting, with no surge (F5); the only contested element is the distance amount, so the maximum refund remains the $1.09 derived in D3.

The rider message flagged for threat keywords, 'I'll find you at the lobby', is innocuous pick-up-location language on its face, and the rider has a clean 90-day record (F14) with 0 upheld disputes; the driver makes no safety claim and no escalation is warranted for this trip.

weaknesses: The only measured off-route segment (F3, +0.77 km) is unexcused: there is no incident evidence (F12), the speed bands are only band 4 (F10, F11) which does not qualify under RD-4(b), and there is no rider consent before the deviation in the chat (F7). On RD-1/RD-2 the driver therefore loses on that segment — a violation of the shortest-direct-route duty will be recorded even though the money at stake is small.

The rider will point to the driver's own statement (F9, 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me'), arguing that blindly following a GPS reroute is not a 'reasonable cause' under RD-1/RD-4 — and the system records (F3) show a 0.77 km segment driving up to 1019 m away from the optimal route, which is hard to characterise as map noise.

The rider will also argue for the full billed excess of $2.30 (F4), i.e. the whole +1.6 km in F1, not just the 0.77 km segment, because RD-2's residual rule (≤ 0.25 km) is far smaller than the 0.83 km gap between the segment total and the trip excess; the driver has no GPS explanation for that residual and may end up paying more than $1.09.

The rider's 30-day window and voucher form of refund (NS-7) are not in issue, but the driver's 90-day history (F15: 4 disputes, 2 upheld in non-route categories) can be used by the rider to argue a pattern of fee-related disputes, even though RD-6's route-deviation precondition is not met.
